item.title: The Code | Model Boundary as an Architectural Object
item.description:
Reflections on a project. Architecture: router + pipelines (AWS, Claude). We'll consider a relatively simple example familiar to almost everyone who has built an LLM agent for natural language queries to data – whether it's text2sql, an analytical assistant, or a database chatbot. Typically, the agent is tasked with handling everything itself – determining the query type, formulating it, choosing the output format, and deciding whether to issue a disclaimer. This is the essence of an agent and the purpose of the system prompt. The system works flawlessly for a dozen test questions. But problems arise later when questions start coming in different formulations. For example, the same question phrased differently is processed differently – the model interprets the phrase differently, and structurally identical results take on different forms (string, table, graph) without explanation. Or, for the same question phrasing, a disclaimer is sometimes provided and sometimes comes back empty. The first thing usually changed in such cases is adding another rule to the prompt. This helps a few times. Then the new rule contradicts the old ones, and the prompt becomes a collection of patches for specific situations. The instability doesn't disappear; it just hides in the order in which the model applies conflicting instructions. This is where both the problem and its solution lie. The problem is that in the described scenario, no one explicitly decided what part of the system is handled by code and what by the model. It evolved organically during prompt generation. If you ask why the model chooses the output format instead of a developer writing ten lines of ordinary code, there's usually no clear answer. Hence the solution: the boundary between what the code does and what the model does is not an implementation detail but a separate architectural object. If this decision isn't made explicitly, it will still be made by default, and most often not in favor of system stability. Read more

item.title: AI Algorithmic Trading: Noise Analysis
item.description:
The thought of making money with AI has been on my mind for three years. When "agent-based" was only heard in Sergey Brin's interviews, and open-source models were only good for adult bots, I created my first agent using nerve-cli. This utility runs model queries in a loop with access to tools and a target prompt. The agent itself wrote a news scraper, performed sentiment analysis, and provided investment recommendations. Essentially, it was a prototype of News Sentiment Trading. This system produced a final result once out of 10 times, and I only acted on one out of 10 final results. But in 2025, something happened to the market. News analysis stopped yielding the desired results. Armed with neural networks (Claude, DeepSeek, Qwen, and free ones from Opencode), I started looking for a working approach. Did I find it?

item.title: How I Made a Desk Lamp in Blender Using Codex and GPT-6 Astra
item.description:
Last year, I bought a 3D printer and decided to print an organizer for small items. I couldn't find a suitable ready-made model, so I opened Blender to create my own. That's where I got stuck: I was lost among the panels, buttons, and settings and put modeling aside. Recently, I saw examples of working with Blender through Codex and GPT-6 Astra in the community and decided to try again. For my first exercise, I chose a desk lamp: base, stem, arm, and shade. After modeling, I set up materials and lighting, then created a five-second camera orbit. Read more

item.title: 70-year-old retiree released 445 books with ChatGPT. But that's not the interesting part
item.description:
A 70-year-old retiree, Bill Jones, has released 445 books using ChatGPT and earns thousands of dollars from them. However, the more interesting aspect isn't Jones himself, but what this case demonstrates. AI has made content creation cheap and fast. Now, instead of spending a year on one book and hoping it becomes popular, one can release many and see which one takes off. I'm trying to understand what this changes for authors. Read more

item.title: I wrote an AI agent with an AI agent: half a year, 1600 commits, and zero rating
item.description:
I've been in IT for over twenty-five years, almost fifteen of them in Android. It turned out that wasn't enough. My experience hasn't disappeared. I still know the difference between an interface and an abstract class, and between val and var. But working the old way became difficult. Requirements increasingly specified not knowledge of Kotlin and Compose, but the ability to conduct development with AI. Not 'tried Copilot,' but to lead: set tasks, analyze results, notice where the tool confidently lies. Instead of the usual TDD, BDD, DDD, and FDD, AIDD and SDD were heard more and more often. It got to the point where mandatory fields appeared in JIRA cards at work: 'AI usage level' with values 'fully completed by agent' and 'partially completed by agent.' There was no option for 'completed independently.' The hint was clear. There was no turning back; it was time to change. Learning from articles made no sense – everything works out there. I needed a real project, large enough to make mistakes in. I didn't choose the topic by chance. I wanted to understand not only how to use AI agents but also how to build them. That's how it happened: I wrote an agent using an agent. The result was an application. Six months later, it's on Google Play, I use it every day, and it's long past being a learning project. What follows is how it grew from there: through three course changes (learning project became a product, Gemini CLI was replaced by Claude Code, a two-output router became a graph), one wall I hit at full speed, and a launch that didn't work. Read more

item.title: +240% Commits, +30% Releases: Agents Hit the SDLC Wall
item.description:
A recent NBER study estimates the cumulative effect of AI tools: up to 240% more commits, but only 30% more releases. Meanwhile, LinkedIn had to build a separate platform for AI code review, and developer surveys show a shift from writing code to verifying results. This article explores why generation speed is no longer the main bottleneck and what kind of engineering system is needed around agents: specifications, shared context, constraints, checks, and metrics all the way to release. Read on.

item.title: How much does a month with an AI agent cost: API vs. subscriptions
item.description:
I calculated the cost of a developer working with an AI agent for a month based on API and subscription prices for September 2026: from $87 on DeepSeek to $7,720 on GPT-6 Astra. Why 82% of tokens are cache, what breaks caching mid-session, why subscription limits in requests are misleading, and how much Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode Go, GLM Coding Plan, and Ollama Cloud actually provide. item.title: Forty rounds of review on code that had already been reviewed: what two AI reviewers found in each other
item.description:
Skillmem code underwent two independent reviews, and I thought it was clean. Then two models, Claude and GPT, read it hostilely for forty consecutive rounds, tasked with reproducing every finding as a team. Six P1s and about twenty-five P2s in code that "had already been reviewed," and the main lesson: every second fix created a regression that only the next round caught. Read more

item.title: The Empire of Terminators: How Two Hundred Agents Built a Civilization
item.description:
In 1959, entomologist Pierre-Paul Grassé studied how termites build their nests, which can reach several meters in height. Each insect carried clay and placed it in a specific location chosen by the swarm leader. Thanks to their collective effort, the termite mounds were intricately designed with ventilation shafts and basements. This phenomenon was termed 'stigmergy'—the coordination of beings through environmental modification. Decades later, researchers at MIT recreated this mechanism in a digital world. Instead of termites, they used AI agents, and instead of termite mounds, they built a technological civilization. This article discusses the results of this 'mini-terminator' experiment and what we humans can learn from LLMs.

item.title: How I Searched for Growing Products on Marketplaces and What AI Has to Do With It
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Ekaterina Nakonechnaya, and I am a product manager at Lenta tech (the IT brand of the Lenta Group). While you can endlessly study product cards, reviews, and competitor prices on marketplaces, it's not enough to understand which products are in growing demand and what should be added to the assortment. In retail, the winner is the one who brings products that customers need right now to the shelves faster and more accurately. Intuition is important, but without prompt analytics, it's easy to make mistakes. Thus, our Advanced Technology Service (ATS), together with the Commerce Service, has successfully piloted the "AI Trends Platform" solution. This product collects sales, search demand, reviews, ratings, and product dynamics from Ozon, Wildberries, and Yandex.Market in a single interface, and then helps filter out positions with potential.
